q: What are `scores` and `passed` after this runs?
code:
const scores = [42, 88, 67, 95];
const passed = scores.filter((s) => s >= 60);
explain: `filter` builds a **new** array of the original items for which the callback returned `true`, and leaves the input alone. It doesn't return the booleans (that would be `map((s) => s >= 60)`), and it doesn't return a count (that would be `passed.length`).

q: A teammate's code returns `[undefined, undefined, undefined]`. Which bug is this?
code:
const names = ["ada", "linus", "grace"];
const loud = names.map((n) => { n.toUpperCase(); });
options: The arrow has a block body `{ … }` with no `return`, so each call returns `undefined`
`toUpperCase` changes the string in place and returns nothing
The callback needs a type annotation `(n: string)`
explain: With braces, an arrow function is a normal function body and only returns what you `return`. Either drop the braces, `(n) => n.toUpperCase()`, or write `{ return n.toUpperCase(); }`. Strings can't be changed in place at all, so `toUpperCase` returns a new string. The annotation is optional, since TypeScript infers `n: string` from the array.

q: Given `function countWhere(items: Song[], test: (s: Song) => boolean): number` and `type Song = { title: string; seconds: number }`, which calls compile? Select all that apply.
explain: The callback type says: you get a `Song`, you must return a `boolean`. The first two do exactly that. `s.year` doesn't exist on `Song`, so the third fails. The fourth returns a `number`, and `number` isn't assignable to `boolean`. TypeScript won't let a truthy-or-falsy number stand in for a real yes/no answer here.

q: `["1", "7", "11"].map(parseInt)` gives `[1, NaN, 3]`. Put the calls that `map` makes in the order they happen.
explain: `map` calls its callback with `(item, index, array)`, once per item, in order. `parseInt` happens to take a second parameter, the radix (number base), so it receives the **index** as the base. The fix is to write the callback yourself so only the item gets passed: `.map((s) => parseInt(s, 10))`.
